summary: Defines the architecture of Netnews systems and how software that creates, distributes, stores and displays articles should treat them. It also sets requirements for any protocol that transports or serves Netnews articles.

eli5.summary: Netnews posts travel between many servers like notes passed around a school. This note explains how those servers and readers should work together and what rules they follow.

questions: how does usenet article propagation work
what is a path header in netnews
how do netnews control messages work
subtitle: The rules every Netnews server, poster, moderator and gateway follows so an article spreads once and arrives unchanged.

tldr.problem: Netnews copies articles between many servers by flooding, with no central authority. Without shared rules, articles would be duplicated, altered, looped back by gateways or forged through control messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5537 gives each role a checklist: posting, injecting, relaying and serving agents, moderators and gateways. It defines the Path trace, duplicate suppression by message identifier, moderation approval, three media types and the control messages.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1036 and RFC 1849, and RFC 8315 updates it. It admits that control messages have no standard authentication, so each agent decides locally what to honor.

today: RFC 5537 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2009. It obsoletes RFC 1036 and RFC 1849, and it is updated by RFC 8315.

sections.title: What Netnews Is and Covers
sections.content:
Netnews is a set of protocols for generating, storing and retrieving news articles and exchanging them among a widely spread readership. It is organized around newsgroups, and the protocols most commonly use a flooding algorithm that propagates copies throughout a network of participating servers. Typically only one copy is stored per server, and each server serves it on demand to its readers.

Usenet is one worldwide, public network built on these protocols. The RFC points out that other deployments exist, such as ones internal to an organization, so it describes the general architecture. The article format itself is in RFC 5536, which should be read alongside it.

The RFC leaves the transport open. NNTP is the most common one, and UUCP and physically delivered magnetic and optical media are named as others. Whatever carries the articles must treat them as uninterpreted octets, except that the NUL octet may not occur and CR LF may appear only as a pair marking a line end. Transports must convey header fields unmodified, and those between relaying and serving agents must convey lines longer than 998 characters.
sections.eli5: Netnews is a giant bulletin board copied onto many computers. The RFC says how the copies are made and passed around, and it does not care whether the notes travel by wire or by mail truck.

sections.title: The Agents and Their Roles
sections.content:
A news server plays up to three roles. An injecting agent accepts a proto-article and starts it on its way. A relaying agent accepts articles from other relaying or injecting agents and passes them on. A serving agent stores articles and makes them available to readers. A user agent is either a posting agent, which helps a person prepare a proto-article, or a reading agent, which fetches articles to show them.

The RFC walks through the life of a typical article: prepared by a posting agent, given to an injecting agent, passed through relaying agents, accepted by a serving agent and finally read. Articles for moderated groups take an extra detour. Many servers combine all three server roles in one program, and the requirements of every role still apply.

Two principles guide it all. The Robustness Principle says to be liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you send, which in practice means rejecting bad articles early and being strict as a poster. The Hippocratic Principle, "First, do no harm", reflects that a small mistake can be amplified by thousands of hosts within minutes. No agent is ever required to accept an article, and agents other than moderators MUST NOT modify articles except as described. Unacceptable articles are rejected rather than corrected.
sections.eli5: Think of a mail chain: one person writes the letter, one stamps it and sends it off, some pass it along, and one puts it in the town library. Everybody has a small job, and nobody is allowed to change what the letter says.

sections.title: Posting, Injecting, Relaying and Serving
sections.content:
A posting agent builds a proto-article, which is a normal article that may omit Message-ID, Date and Path and must not contain Injection-Info or Xref. It must never create an Injection-Info header. For followups, the References header is built from the parent's References plus the parent's Message-ID. If it would exceed 998 characters it MUST be trimmed, and the first identifier and the last two must stay.

The injecting agent carries the main responsibility for conformance. It rejects syntactically invalid proto-articles, should reject articles dated more than 24 hours in the future, adds a missing Message-ID and Date, must not alter the body, updates Path, and should add Injection-Info. It adds an Injection-Date only if the proto-article had no Message-ID and Date pair. Articles for moderated groups without an Approved header are forwarded to a moderator instead.

A relaying agent rejects articles missing Newsgroups, Message-ID or a date, rejects dates more than 24 hours ahead, rejects anything it has already accepted, updates Path and may touch only Path and Xref. A serving agent does similar checks, must reject unapproved articles in moderated groups, removes any Xref and normally adds its own, then stores the article. It must not create a newsgroup just because an unknown name appears. Reading agents have no specific protocol requirements.
sections.eli5: The sender can leave some boxes blank on the form, and the first post office fills them in. After that, every stop checks the stamp, refuses duplicates, and only adds its own mark on the outside.

sections.title: The Path Trail and Duplicate Suppression
sections.content:
Because servers flood articles to many peers, each may be offered the same article several times. Relaying and serving agents therefore MUST keep a history of articles already seen and reject repeats, identified by message identifier. To keep that record from growing forever, agents may choose a cutoff interval and reject articles dated before it. For Usenet a cutoff of no less than seven days is conventional. If history is dropped by the date an article was first seen, the retention interval MUST be at least 24 hours longer than the cutoff.

Every server component that handles an article prepends its path-identity to the Path header, so the header is built from right to left. The preferred identity is the machine's fully qualified domain name. Between identities, a diagnostic records how the sender was checked: !.POSTED marks the point of injection, a doubled !! means the expected identity matched, !.MISMATCH. means it did not, and !.SEEN. means the agent did not check. Older software adds only a single !.

The same trail helps avoid waste: an article SHOULD NOT be relayed to a server whose identity already appears in its Path.
sections.eli5: Every stop signs the back of the note, so a server can see where it has been and skip a note it already has. Each stop also writes whether it trusts the one before it.

sections.title: Moderators and Gateways
sections.content:
For a moderated group, the injecting agent forwards the proto-article to the moderator of the leftmost moderated group, customarily by email. Two ways exist: encapsulate it as application/news-transmission with usage=moderate, or send it as a plain email. The first has technical advantages, but the second is more common, so the first SHOULD NOT be used unless the moderator is known to handle it. A moderator who approves adds an Approved header, removes any Injection-Date, Injection-Info and Xref, truncates Path, and passes the article to an injecting agent. If several moderated groups are involved, the article goes round each moderator in turn.

A gateway converts articles to or from another medium, such as email, or conveys them between two separate Netnews networks. Its great danger is loops that repeatedly reinject an article. Incoming gateways MUST NOT gate the same message twice, must produce valid proto-articles, must hand them to an injecting agent, and must add a Sender header with the administrator's mailbox. Any original Sender is renamed to the new Original-Sender header, which this RFC registers.

The RFC's worked example guards a mailing-list gateway with several layers: preserve message identifiers, mark generated mail with an X-* header the other gateway discards, and refuse messages whose Path contains the list server name. It also advises making a group moderated when it is gated both ways to a mailing list.
sections.eli5: A moderator is like a teacher who reads each note before it goes on the class board. A gateway is a translator between the board and some other mailbox, and it has to be careful not to hand a note back and forth forever.

sections.title: Media Types and Control Messages
sections.content:
Three media types are registered. application/news-transmission wraps a complete article for mailing to a moderator, injecting agent or relaying agent, with an optional usage parameter. application/news-groupinfo carries a group name, description and moderation status for a newgroup message. application/news-checkgroups lists every group in a hierarchy. The old message/news type is declared obsolete in favor of message/rfc822.

A control message is an article with a Control header. The standard group controls are newgroup, rmgroup and checkgroups, and all MUST carry an Approved header or SHOULD NOT be honored. checkgroups may have a scope list, where a ! prefix excludes a sub-hierarchy, and an increasing serial number, as in checkgroups de !de.alt #2009021301. A cancel message withdraws an article by message identifier, and a Supersedes header is treated the same way. The ihave and sendme messages are a predecessor of NNTP and largely obsolete. sendsys, version, whogets and senduuname are declared obsolete. A subject starting with cmsg no longer makes an article a control message.
sections.eli5: Control messages are special notes that tell a server to do something, like start a new club or throw away a note. Each server is free to say no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that Netnews offers little security. What protection exists against abuse and impersonation comes mainly from the underlying transport. Where servers cannot enforce authentication, articles can be trivially forged and widely read.

Control messages are the main worry, since unauthorized ones can remove newsgroups, delete articles or create unwanted groups. There is no standardized way to authenticate them, only unstandardized practices such as PGP-based signing, so agents SHOULD authenticate them by local policy, and many sites currently ignore all cancels and Supersedes headers. Article contents must be treated as potentially malicious: some servers have been attacked through Unix shell code in the Control header. A poster may fake an Approved header to bypass moderation, or put a site's identity in Path to keep an article from reaching it, which the POSTED marker helps prevent.

For leakage, restricted distribution depends on the goodwill of every receiving site. The flooding algorithm is extremely good at finding a way out of a restricted subnet, and the advice is to designate a small number of gateways for outside exchange.
sections.eli5: A bulletin board anyone can write on is easy to fake. Special "do something" notes are the riskiest, so each server should check who really sent them before obeying.

sections.title: Changes From Earlier Practice
sections.content:
The RFC records a twelve-year effort by the USEFOR Working Group, with the draft by Henry Spencer as its initial basis. Appendix A lists what changed from the protocol described in RFC 1036. The notable items are a new backward-compatible Path format, required trimming of References, the new Injection-Date header, the new media types and the obsolete control messages.

Cancel messages no longer need From and Sender headers matching the target, since that requirement added no real security. The relayer name in ihave and sendme is now required, and checkgroups gained two optional parameters. Many steps that RFC 1036 left unmentioned but servers widely implemented are now written down in detail.
sections.eli5: This part is the list of rule changes since the old rule book, plus a thank-you to the many people who spent years writing the new one.

items.label: Create a group
items.desc: Creates a group or changes its moderation status or description.

items.label: Remove a group
items.desc: Removes a group from the server's list of valid groups.

items.label: Check a hierarchy
items.desc: Lists all valid groups in a hierarchy with descriptions and moderation status.

items.label: Withdraw an article
items.desc: Withdraws a target article identified by its message identifier.

items.label: Offer articles
items.desc: States that the named relaying agent has articles with the listed identifiers.

items.label: Request articles
items.desc: Asks the receiver to send the listed articles to the named relaying agent.
